newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries snub US budget talk to focus on economy.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries snub US budget talk to focus on economy.

text.p: The U.S. budget sparring that could grab the Treasury market's attention a year and a half ago barely elicits a nod this year, now that investors have shifted their attention to the ramifications of a strong U.S. economy, analysts said.

On Thursday, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott fired off a few shots at President Clinton's budget plan, saying that he would not participate in a budget "fraud" and that the more he looked at the President's budget, the less he saw in it.

But the shots fired on Capital Hill did not resound on Wall Street, where the bond market was in retreat -- again -- amid fears of a tight labor market and new concern that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates on March 25.

Analysts said a Reuters story attributed to some Fed watchers and to a source close to the Fed intensified those concerns. The story said the Fed was likely to tighten credit at its March 25 meeting to safeguard the conditions that would allow the U.S. expansion to sail into its seventh year.

Especially on the eve of the February U.S. employment report but even in general, the market's preoccupation with a strong economy and the possibility of a Fed tightening has pushed a budget deal to the back of the bus in terms of financial market considerations, analysts said.

"Twenty-four hours ahead of the payrolls report, people don't care what Trent Lott says," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets. "There are so many other things on the market's mind: employment, what the Fed will do. The budget has become a detail. It's crazy to even consider it an issue."

"The budget is not on the front burner as an issue for the financial markets," agreed Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "People are tuning out the rhetoric, (but) might focus on issues when negotiators get closer to resolution."
One reason a budget deal has lost some importance is that federal budget deficits have been shrinking, analysts said.

"Our budget deficit is less than 1.5 percent of (Gross Domestic Product)," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "That more than meets the Maastricht criteria."
The Maastricht criteria are the economic guidelines that countries must meet in order to qualify for participation in the launch of a single European currency in 1999.
"We're doing three times better on reducing the federal budget deficit than the European countries struggling to meet the Maastricht criteria," he said.

The U.S. reaction to the federal budget debate is now, "So what? Who cares?," Karydakis said. "Nobody thinks about the balanced budget. The world has changed. Markets are dynamic and the focus changes very quickly."
On Thursday, the financial markets' focus undoubtedly was the February U.S. payrolls report due Friday.

The bond market is most concerned with the tightness in the labor market which was underscored by Thursday's jobless claims data, said Williams. The Labor Department reported new jobless claims fell to 310,000 in the week ended March 1 from 316,000 a week earlier.

"The labor market doesn't get much tighter than this," said Williams. "That provides the context for concern about tomorrow's February employment report. That's what is weighing on the market the most today."
